title: What do the other two groups of angles share?
description: Three groups of angles are drawn, and the middle group holds right angles. An L shaped paper corner is laid on every angle of the other two groups to see how each one compares with a right angle. Keeko's doubt, that short arms make the angles alike, is broken by making the arms longer.
teaching_notes: One idea: compare every angle with a right angle; smaller ones are acute, and bigger ones that stay under a straight angle are obtuse. Watch for children who judge an angle by the length of its arms.

source: Angles are classified in three groups as shown (a box with t
video_script.why: The child learns to sort angles by comparing each one with a right angle, and meets the names acute and obtuse.
video_script.substitution: An L shaped paper corner is laid on each angle of the first and third groups.
video_script.anchor: the book's box of angles sorted into three groups, with right angles in the middle group
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko compares the length of the arms instead of the opening between them.
video_script.payoff_line: Angles smaller than a right angle are called acute. Angles between a right angle and a straight angle are called obtuse.

final_answer.value: first group: less than a right angle (acute); third group: more than a right angle but less than a straight angle (obtuse)
final_answer.spoken: the first group holds angles smaller than a right angle, called acute, and the third group holds angles bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight angle, called obtuse

maths_rules: middle group: right angles, each fits the L shaped corner exactly, a quarter turn
first group: each angle fits inside the corner, so it is smaller than a right angle, less than a quarter turn
third group: each angle is wider than the corner but narrower than a straight angle, so more than a quarter turn and less than a half turn
longer arms do not change the opening, so arm length does not decide the kind of angle
